derivations.claim: In uniform mode, for any block start $x_a$, deterministic replay reproduces the original $x_{a+1},\ldots,x_b$: the first replayed transition starts from the identical $x_a$, and induction applies each same map $F_j$ to the same preceding state. Thus the recorded local tape at step $\ell$ has the same primitive inputs as the original forward trajectory, so its reverse rule is the same one used by the full tape. Processing blocks and then their steps in decreasing order is exactly reverse transition order; [F2] gives the same terminal and initial cotangents.

A block of length $r$ has replay prefix lengths $r-1,r-2,\ldots,0$ before its $r$ recorded local evaluations. Therefore its additional unrecorded evaluations total $\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}j=r(r-1)/2$. The number of blocks is $s=\lceil T/q\rceil\le m$, each $r_\ell\le q$, so the sum is at most $m q(q-1)/2$. The checkpoint indices are $0,q,\ldots,(s-1)q<T$; $T/q\le m$, so $s=\lceil T/q\rceil\le m$. Only those states, one live state, and one local tape are retained.

In binomial mode the recurrence and boundary values give $C(d,t)=\binom{d+t}{d}$: the binomial coefficients have the same boundary values and Pascal recurrence, so induction on $d+t$ identifies them. For $d,t\ge1$, write $A=C(d,t-1)$, $B=C(d-1,t)$, so $C(d,t)=A+B$. If $N\ge2$, $L=\min(N-1,A)$ satisfies $1\le L<N$; if $L=N-1$, then $R=1\le B$, and otherwise $L=A$ and $R=N-A\le B$. Thus both recursive capacities hold and both child lengths are strictly less than $N$; the recursion terminates at $N=1$ or $N=0$.

Induct on $N$. The base calls $N=0,1$ do no transition or apply one recorded transition's reverse rule. For $N\ge2$, the midpoint replay produces the exact $x_{a+L}$ by [F3]. The right child returns the exact cotangent at that midpoint by induction. The left child then applies the remaining earlier transitions to that cotangent, so the chain rule gives the exact cotangent at $x_a$. Every interval is split into disjoint left and right steps and each base step is recorded and reversed once. Therefore the terminal value and initial cotangent agree with the ordinary reverse sweep.

During a right child, the saved midpoint occupies one slot and its child uses at most $d-1$ further snapshots; after that child returns, the midpoint is released and the left child uses at most $d$. Thus peak snapshot count is at most $d$. A step in a right child has at most $t$ replays by induction. A step in the left child is replayed once at the current split and then has at most $t-1$ replays in the left child, hence at most $t$ total. Each step also has one recorded forward and one reverse call, giving work $\widehat W+\overline W+tW$. Each recursive child decreases $d+t$ by one, so at most $d+t+1$ call frames are active; each frame stores a fixed number of scalar indices and flags. The algorithm reuses its cotangent buffer and has only the bounded one-step tape and local scratch included in $G$. The saved states and one live primal state use at most $(d+1)R_s$ scalar entries, giving storage at most $G+(d+1)R_s$.

The same finite recurrence with $\widetilde A_e$ yields the sum of perturbed path products. By [F2], the exact path sum is $g_i$.

Fix a path $\pi=(e_1,\ldots,e_s)$. Insert one factor at a time to write
$$\widetilde A_{e_s}\cdots\widetilde A_{e_1}-A_{e_s}\cdots A_{e_1}=\sum_{\ell=1}^s\widetilde A_{e_s}\cdots\widetilde A_{e_{\ell+1}}(\widetilde A_{e_\ell}-A_{e_\ell})A_{e_{\ell-1}}\cdots A_{e_1}.$$
This identity follows by cancellation of consecutive products in the telescoping sum.

Submultiplicativity of the induced operator norm and [A1] bound the $\ell$th summand by $\eta_{e_\ell}\prod_{r<\ell}\|A_{e_r}\|\prod_{r>\ell}(\|A_{e_r}\|+\eta_{e_r})$. Summing these bounds over $\ell$ controls the error on this path.

The perturbed and exact gradients are finite sums over the same paths by step 1.1. The triangle inequality therefore bounds their difference by the sum of the pathwise errors from step 2.1, which is exactly the displayed bound.

derivations.claim: For $x>0$, the active formula is $f(x)=x$, whose derivative is $1$; for $x<0$, the active formula is $f(x)=-x$, whose derivative is $-1$. These are the two derivatives used by the strict-branch rule in [F1].
At zero, the right difference quotient is $(|h|-0)/h=1$ for $h>0$, while the left quotient is $(|h|-0)/h=-1$ for $h<0$. Since the one-sided limits differ, the derivative does not exist at zero.
By [F1], the branch boundary therefore returns NONDIFFERENTIABLE and no derivative; selecting a generalized derivative would require a separately supplied rule.

citations.quote:
Let $R:\Theta\times Z\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^1$, where $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $Z\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ are open. Suppose $R(\theta_0,z_0)=0$ and the state Jacobian $R_z(\theta_0,z_0)$ is invertible. The Euclidean implicit function theorem gives a local $C^1$ solution branch $z=\phi(\theta)$, and
$$D\phi(\theta_0)=-R_z(\theta_0,z_0)^{-1}R_\theta(\theta_0,z_0).$$
For a scalar $C^1$ objective $J(\theta,z)$, its derivative along that branch is
$$D(J(\theta,\phi(\theta)))|_{\theta_0}=J_\theta-J_zR_z^{-1}R_\theta.$$
Equivalently, if $\lambda$ solves $R_z^T\lambda=J_z^T$, this derivative is $J_\theta-\lambda^TR_\theta$. These formulas concern the exact local solution branch; differentiating a stopped iteration is a separate finite-map derivative.

For the real mathematical solve primitive $\phi(A,b)=A^{-1}b$, let $A,B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $b,\widehat x\in\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge1$, and suppose certified exact-residual bounds satisfy
$$\|I-AB\|_2\le d<1,\qquad \|b-A\widehat x\|_2\le\rho,\qquad \|B\|_2\le M,\qquad K=\frac{M}{1-d}.$$
Then $A$ is invertible; writing $x=A^{-1}b$, the fixed linear derivative approximations $\widetilde J_bh=Bh$ and $\widetilde J_AH=-BH\widehat x$ obey
$$\|\widetilde J_b-J_b\|\le\eta_b=Kd,\qquad \|\widetilde J_A-J_A\|\le\eta_A=Kd\|\widehat x\|_2+K^2\rho.$$
Use Euclidean vector norms and Frobenius matrix-input norm. Their adjoints are $B^Tc$ and $-(B^Tc)\widehat x^T$. If these adjoints are evaluated by successful length-$n$ rounded real dots and componentwise outer products, put $t=\gamma_n\|B\|_F$, assuming $nu<1$. The resulting cotangent errors are bounded by $(\eta_b+t)\|c\|_2$ and $[\eta_A+(t+u(M+t))\|\widehat x\|_2]\|c\|_2$, respectively. These are derivative approximations to the mathematical solve map, not derivatives of the rounded program.

The fixed $B$ may be assembled from stored basis-vector solves using a triangular, Cholesky or QR backend; its defect must be certified rather than inferred from a factor residual. Replay must preserve the same $\widehat x,B$ and strict graph branch. Reverse accumulation additions are excluded.

derivations.claim: The system gives $u_2=1$ and $u_1+\theta u_2=2$, hence $u(\theta)=(2-\theta,1)^T$ and $J(\theta)=3-\theta$. Therefore $J'(0)=-1$.
Write $R(u,\theta)=A(\theta)u-b$. At $\theta=0$, $u=(2,1)^T$, $R_u=A(0)=I$, $R_\theta=A_\theta u=(1,0)^T$, and $J_u=(1,1)$. The adjoint equation $R_u^T\lambda=J_u^T$ gives $\lambda=(1,1)^T$.
The objective has no explicit $\theta$ dependence, so $J_\theta=0$; the adjoint formula gives $J_\theta-\lambda^TR_\theta=-(1,1)\cdot(1,0)=-1$.
The adjoint result agrees with the direct derivative in step 1.1, verifying this nonsingular linear-solve instance.

In any arithmetic satisfying the operationwise model and representing $0,1,2,3$, with these small operations in range, at $\theta=0$ the primal and basis solves give $\widehat x=(2,1)^T$ and $B=I$ exactly. Their inverse defect and primal residual are zero. The certified solve-Jacobian result [[lem-certified-linear-solve-jacobian-and-pullback-error]] therefore gives zero fixed-map discrepancy; the actual dot and product operations here are also exact, and return derivative $-1$.

Seed $\bar x_2=1$. At step $k=1$, $\partial x_2/\partial x_1=1+h\alpha=3/2$ and $\partial x_2/\partial\alpha=h x_1=3/4$, so $\bar x_1=3/2$ and the accumulated $\bar\alpha=3/4$.

The reverse result equals the direct derivative in step 1.1, and [F2] identifies it as the derivative of the finite trajectory map.

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, $x\in\mathbb F^n$, $y\in\mathbb F^m$ have stored real or complex entries, with $m,n\ge1$. Use the operationwise arithmetic model, successful sequential dot products, and $0<u<1$ with $(\max(m,n)-1)u<1$. Define
$$g_k=\frac{1+6u}{1-(k-1)u}-1,\qquad F=\|A\|_F,\quad X=\|x\|_2,\quad Y=\|y\|_2.$$
For $\widehat v=\operatorname{fl}(Ax)$ and $\widehat w=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat v-y)$, put $V=g_nFX$ and $W=V+u(\|\widehat v\|_2+Y)$. Then
$$\|\widehat w-(Ax-y)\|_2\le W.$$
For a stored real $\lambda>0$, also compute $\widehat z=\operatorname{fl}(A^*\widehat w)$, $\widehat l=\operatorname{fl}(\lambda x)$ and $\widehat r=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat z+\widehat l)$, rounding scalar multiplication componentwise. The exact intended normal residual $r=A^*(Ax-y)+\lambda x$ satisfies
$$\|\widehat r-r\|_2\le\rho:=FW+g_mF\|\widehat w\|_2+u\lambda X+u(\|\widehat z\|_2+\|\widehat l\|_2).$$
Norms in these certificates mean exact norms or certified upper bounds. Uncontrolled rounding of the certificate itself is not authorized. The linear bound applies columnwise to certify $\|I-AB\|_2\le\|I-AB\|_F$ from stored basis-solve columns $B$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

derivations.claim: For every $z$, $\|ABz\|\ge(1-d)\|z\|$. Thus [F3] makes $AB$, hence both square factors, invertible and gives $\|(AB)^{-1}\|\le1/(1-d)$. Since $A^{-1}=B(AB)^{-1}$, $\|A^{-1}\|\le K$. The identity $B-A^{-1}=A^{-1}(AB-I)$ gives $\|B-A^{-1}\|\le Kd$, while $\widehat x-x=A^{-1}(A\widehat x-b)$ gives $\|\widehat x-x\|\le K\rho$. The residuals in these identities are exact; [F2] explains how to certify them from rounded evaluations.

Apply [F1] at the exact point $(A,b)$. For the matrix edge, $BH\widehat x-A^{-1}Hx=(B-A^{-1})H\widehat x+A^{-1}H(\widehat x-x)$. Since $\|H\|_2\le\|H\|_F$, step 1.1 gives $\eta_A$; the vector edge gives $\eta_b$. Taking Euclidean/Frobenius adjoints yields the stated pullbacks with the same norm discrepancies. This explicitly accounts for the perturbed primal evaluation point through $\rho$.

Real dot-product coefficient expansion bounds $\|\widehat\lambda-B^Tc\|_2\le t\|c\|_2$, hence $\|\widehat\lambda\|_2\le(M+t)\|c\|_2$. Each rounded outer-product entry has error at most $u|\widehat\lambda_i\widehat x_j|$, so its Frobenius error is at most $u(M+t)\|\widehat x\|_2\|c\|_2$. Combine these with step 1.2 and the contribution $t\|\widehat x\|_2\|c\|_2$ from the rounded adjoint solve.

For each realized nonzero $c$, any cotangent error vector $z$ is the action on $c$ of the linear map $zc^T/\|c\|^2$, whose induced norm is $\|z\|/\|c\|$; vectorize the matrix cotangent for the matrix edge. When $c=0$, successful operations return exact zero. Thus the realized rounded pullbacks admit local linear-map perturbations with the displayed bounds, without asserting global linearity of rounding. The graph perturbation theorem may propagate these realized maps with exact accumulation.
